title: Identity Federation
description: Build identity federation for multi-tenant SaaS applications and understand trust relationships between identity systems.

data.text: **Identity Federation** is the trust relationship between two identity domains that allows users from one domain to access resources in another. In a multi-tenant SaaS application, federation enables each customer (tenant) to use their own identity provider — such as Azure AD, Okta, or Google Workspace — while your application treats them all through a unified interface.

data.caption: Multi-tenant federation where each tenant connects their own identity provider to the SaaS application.
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant SP as SaaS App
    participant IdP as Tenant IdP (Azure AD / Okta)
    U->>SP: Visit app.myapp.com/tenant-a
    SP->>SP: Detect tenant from domain or subdomain
    SP->>U: Redirect to Tenant A's IdP
    U->>IdP: Authenticate with corporate credentials
    IdP->>U: Return SAML/OIDC assertion
    U->>SP: Present assertion
    SP->>SP: Validate against Tenant A's metadata
    SP->>U: Logged into Tenant A workspace

cards.title: B2B Federation
cards.description: Business-to-business trust where partner organizations access your application using their corporate IdP.
cons: Support burden for multiple IdP types

cards.title: B2C Federation
cards.description: Business-to-consumer federation allowing consumers to use social or email identities.

data.text: The core technical challenge in federated SaaS is routing each authentication request to the correct identity provider. Common strategies include subdomain-based routing (tenant-a.app.com), email domain matching (users @acme.com go to Acme's IdP), or a pre-login tenant selection page. Once the tenant is identified, your application loads the appropriate metadata, initiates the correct protocol flow, and validates the assertion against the tenant-specific configuration.

data.title: Tenant-aware authentication middleware
data.content: Resolve the tenant from the hostname and store it for the authentication handler.

data.title: SAML Metadata Best Practices
items: Store IdP metadata XML per tenant in a database or secure blob storage.
Refresh metadata on a schedule (e.g., every 24 hours) to capture certificate rotations.
Validate metadata signatures before trusting federation data.
Cache metadata aggressively to avoid network calls during authentication.
Alert when a tenant's signing certificate is nearing expiry.

data.title: Metadata Refresh Is Critical
data.text: Enterprise IdPs rotate certificates periodically. If your SaaS application caches metadata indefinitely, authentication will fail silently when a certificate expires. Implement background metadata refresh with monitoring and alerting.

When a user authenticates via federation for the first time, your application must create a local user account or link the external identity to an existing account. This process is called Just-In-Time provisioning. The external identity provider supplies attributes like email, name, and groups. Your application maps these to local roles and permissions. Be cautious with group mapping — always validate that the incoming group claims match expected values for the tenant to prevent privilege escalation.

data.title: Handling federated user creation on login
data.content: Create or update a local user profile when a federated user signs in.

data.title: Federation Security Checklist
items: Validate the AudienceRestriction in SAML assertions against the expected tenant entity ID.
Replay-protect SAML assertions by caching used InResponseTo values.
Verify token signatures using the correct tenant-specific public key.
Rate-limit authentication endpoints to prevent brute-force attacks against the IdP.
Log federation events (login, provisioning, errors) for audit and debugging.
Enforce HTTPS for all metadata endpoints and callback URLs.

data.title: Replay Attacks
data.text: SAML assertions can be replayed if intercepted. Always check that the AssertionID or InResponseTo value has not been seen before. Store processed IDs in a short-lived cache (e.g., Redis with TTL).

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Federation connects separate identity systems through trust relationships
B2B federation uses enterprise IdPs; B2C uses social or database providers
Dynamic provider selection is essential for multi-tenant SaaS
Metadata must be refreshed to handle certificate rotations
JIT provisioning creates local accounts on first federated login
Always validate audience, signatures, and replay-protect SAML assertions
data.takeaway: Identity federation turns a single-tenant application into a multi-tenant platform, but it requires careful tenant isolation, metadata management, and security validation.
